vignette: The desert sun burns behind his eyelids, hot and unyielding, the same way it did the day the ground gave way. He stands in the memory as he has stood in it for decades: the air thick with grit and diesel, the sudden crack of rifle fire splitting the morning, the heavy thud of a young teammate collapsing into his grip. He drags him across the hardpan, counting steps, counting breaths, counting the seconds until the medevac's rotors finally break the sky. The teammate's hand goes slack. The official report calls it a successful extraction. He calls it the moment the earth stopped holding him up. For forty years, he has built his life on structure. He learns to fly before he learns to trust his own nervous system. The cockpit becomes a sanctuary of checklists, radio frequencies, and predictable algorithms. Flying keeps the noise at bay, but the noise never leaves. It waits. Now, at sixty-three, he still pins the silver wings to his left breast pocket each morning. On pre-flight briefings, he runs through the walk-arounds with mechanical precision, but his fingers tremble when he touches the overhead panel. The first rule of flight is to trust the instruments, yet his body betrays him the moment the tires leave the runway. At thirty thousand feet, the engine's steady hum sometimes warps into the low, rhythmic thrum of a helicopter's chase. He adjusts the trim a fraction too early, catches himself, and resets his hands on the yoke. His co-pilot notices the pause, asks if everything is fine, and he answers with a flat, practiced, "All good." He does not mention the cold sweat tracing his spine or the way his jaw locks until his teeth ache. At home, the television volume stays perpetually low. Sudden bangs-the microwave finishing, a dropped book, a gust against the window-make him flinch so hard his coffee mug rattles against the counter. His wife has learned to announce herself, to tap his shoulder twice before speaking. He loves her deeply, but intimacy feels like a vulnerability he cannot afford. He turns onto his side when she moves closer in bed, her breathing syncopating into a rhythm that suddenly sounds like distant footsteps on dry earth. He tells himself it is just old wiring, a body still expecting an attack that never comes on this quiet suburban street. He carries the navigation traditions of his Pacific lineage, ancestors who read the swells and stars to find shorelines. Yet now, the sky, his professional domain, feels less like a vast horizon and more like a ceiling closing in. He avoids night flights whenever possible, trading his preferred routes for daylight sectors that end by late afternoon. On the tarmac, he stands apart from the crew's laughter, watching the jet bridge retract with a sharp inhale. The metal joints grind, the hydraulic hiss rises, the sudden jolt seals the door-it maps perfectly onto a memory he has spent decades outrunning. He finishes his pre-approach checklist. The runway lights stretch into the distance like illuminated nerve endings. He breathes in, counts to four, and lets it out slow. The plane descends. His hands rest lightly on the controls. He is still here. He will walk out of the aircraft, drive home, and sit at the kitchen table while his wife boils the kettle. He will listen to the water begin to sing and remind himself, as he does every time, that this is not a battlefield, but a Tuesday. The ground will hold him until tomorrow.
